patterns.title: Multi-stage builds
patterns.problem: A single-stage Dockerfile ships the whole build toolchain (compilers, SDKs, source) into the production image, bloating size and attack surface.
patterns.solution: Use multiple FROM statements: build in one stage, then COPY only the runtime artifact into a minimal final stage (or scratch). BuildKit only builds stages your --target depends on.
patterns.anti_pattern: FROM golang then COPY . . and RUN go build, shipping the compiler and source in the final layer.
patterns.snippet:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.26 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY <<EOF ./main.go
package main
import "fmt"
func main() { fmt.Println("hello") }
EOF
RUN go build -o /bin/hello ./main.go
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /bin/hello /bin/hello
CMD ["/bin/hello"]

patterns.title: Healthchecks
patterns.problem: A container reporting 'running' is not necessarily 'ready'; load balancers may route traffic before the app can serve it, causing 502s.
patterns.solution: Define a healthcheck (test/interval/timeout/retries/start_period) so the runtime knows actual readiness, then gate dependents on it.
patterns.anti_pattern: Treating the container 'Up' state as proof the service accepts connections.
patterns.snippet:
healthcheck:
  test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:3000/health"]
  interval: 30s
  timeout: 10s
  retries: 3
  start_period: 40s

patterns.title: Persist database data with named volumes
patterns.problem: Container writable layers are ephemeral — recreating the DB container loses all data.
patterns.solution: Mount a Docker named volume at the engine's data directory (e.g. /var/lib/postgresql/data for Postgres, /data for Redis).
patterns.anti_pattern: Relying on the container's writable layer, or using host bind mounts on Windows (slow I/O and UID/permission errors).
patterns.snippet:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:18.6
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: example
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  pgdata:

patterns.title: Seed/schema-load with docker-entrypoint-initdb.d
patterns.problem: You need an initial schema, users, or seed data created only on first startup.
patterns.solution: Mount .sql/.sh scripts into /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d; the official Postgres/MySQL entrypoints run them once on an empty data dir (alphabetical order).
patterns.anti_pattern: Baking schema into the image (rebuild to change it) or running init manually after every `docker compose up`.
patterns.snippet:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:18.6
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: example
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
    volumes:
      - ./init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d
# ./init/01-schema.sql and ./init/02-seed.sql run once on first init

patterns.title: Cache dependencies (CI)
patterns.problem: Reinstalling dependencies on every run wastes minutes and billable CI time.
patterns.solution: Use actions/cache with a key derived from a lockfile hash so the cache invalidates only when deps change; add restore-keys as fallbacks.
patterns.anti_pattern: Using a constant key (cache never updates) or storing tokens/credentials in the cached path.
patterns.snippet:
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: ${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
    restore-keys: |
      ${{ runner.os }}-npm-

patterns.title: OIDC federated auth (no stored secrets)
patterns.problem: Long-lived cloud credentials stored as GitHub secrets can leak and grant persistent access.
patterns.solution: Set `permissions: id-token: write` and exchange GitHub's OIDC JWT for a short-lived cloud token via the provider's official action.
patterns.anti_pattern: Storing static cloud access keys as secrets; or a trust policy not scoped to a specific repo and ref.
patterns.snippet:
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-oidc
          aws-region: us-east-1

patterns.title: Remote state backend + locking
patterns.problem: Local terraform.tfstate is not shareable across a team, is easy to lose, and concurrent applies cause corruption.
patterns.solution: Store state in a remote backend (e.g. S3) with encryption + versioning, and use a state-locking table (DynamoDB) so only one apply runs at a time.
patterns.anti_pattern: Committing tfstate to git, or a backend with no locking (two engineers apply and clobber state).

patterns.title: Local testing with LocalStack
patterns.problem: Testing Terraform against real AWS is slow and costs money; engineers can't iterate offline.
patterns.solution: Point the AWS provider at LocalStack's endpoint (http://localhost:4566) and run plan/apply/test locally; integrate into CI for fast, free feedback.
patterns.anti_pattern: Only ever applying against live AWS; skipping tests because 'there's no cheap way to try it'.

patterns.title: 12-factor app
patterns.problem: Apps that bake config into code, keep state on disk, or write logs to files become non-portable and can't scale horizontally.
patterns.solution: Store config in the environment (factor III), run as stateless processes that share nothing (factor VI), and stream logs to stdout/stderr as event streams (factor XI).
patterns.anti_pattern: Hardcoding DATABASE_URL in source, writing session state to local disk, or logging to a local file the operator must tail.
patterns.snippet:
image: myapp:1.2.3
environment:
  - DATABASE_URL=${DATABASE_URL}
  - LOG_LEVEL=info
# process logs to stdout; orchestrator collects the stream

patterns.title: GitOps: Git as single source of truth
patterns.problem: Cluster state edited by hand or by divergent CI pipelines drifts from intent and can't be audited or reproduced.
patterns.solution: Declare desired state in Git; a controller continuously reconciles the cluster to the repo, with automated sync, pruning, and self-healing. Changes go through PRs, not kubectl.
patterns.anti_pattern: Manually kubectl apply-ing to prod, or running imperative deploy scripts that bypass the Git record.

tutorials.title: The Twelve-Factor App
tutorials.summary: The canonical 12 factors (config, processes, logs, build/release/run) that underpins most modern cloud-native ops patterns.

methodologies.name: 12-Factor App
methodologies.summary: Methodology for building portable, scalable, cloud-native services: config in env, stateless processes, logs as streams.
methodologies.steps:
1. Store config in environment variables (factor III), never in code
2. Treat backing services (DB, cache) as attached resources via URLs/env
3. Run as stateless processes that share nothing (factor VI)
4. Stream logs to stdout/stderr as event streams (factor XI)
5. Keep build/release/run strictly separated; one codebase per app

methodologies.name: GitOps
methodologies.summary: Git is the single source of truth for desired state; a controller continuously reconciles live infra to the repo.
methodologies.steps:
1. Declare desired cluster/infra state in a Git repository
2. A controller continuously reconciles live state to Git (Argo CD / Flux)
3. All changes via pull requests; no manual kubectl/apply to prod
4. Enable automated sync + prune + self-heal
5. Roll back by reverting the Git commit

methodologies.name: Infrastructure as Code: Plan/Apply + Remote State
methodologies.summary: Declarative infra with reviewed plans and shared, locked state for safe team collaboration.
methodologies.steps:
1. Write infra as declarative HCL (Terraform/OpenTofu)
2. Store state in a remote backend with locking (S3 + DynamoDB)
3. Run `terraform plan` and review the diff before apply
4. Apply only the reviewed plan; gate apply behind PR review
5. Detect drift with `terraform plan -refresh-only` in CI

methodologies.name: Local-First Testing
methodologies.summary: Run dependencies and emulated cloud locally so iteration is offline, fast, and cost-free before touching real cloud.
methodologies.steps:
1. Run dependencies as Docker containers (Postgres, Redis) with named volumes
2. Emulate cloud (AWS) locally with LocalStack at localhost:4566
3. Gate dependents with healthchecks + depends_on: service_healthy
4. Iterate offline; only apply to real cloud after local validation

methodologies.name: Progressive Delivery (blue-green / canary)
methodologies.summary: Reduce deploy risk by shifting traffic gradually and keeping an instant rollback path.
methodologies.steps:
1. Deploy new version alongside old (blue-green) without cutting traffic
2. Validate health, then flip router/selector to green
3. Or shift a small % of traffic (canary) first
4. Ramp as metrics stay healthy; instant rollback by re-flipping

methodologies.name: Immutable Infrastructure
methodologies.summary: Build fully-versioned artifacts once and deploy by replacement, making every version reproducible and rollback trivial.
methodologies.steps:
1. Bake a fully-versioned image/artifact once
2. Deploy by replacing instances, never mutating running ones
3. Use create_before_destroy to avoid downtime
4. Rollback = redeploy the prior image version
